Newly hatched Sardinian brook salamanders exhibit a snout–vent length of approximately 0.479 centimeters [Lb = approximately 0.479 centimeters], a diminutive size reflecting the relatively small, yolk-laden eggs typical of the genus. Egg development and hatching timing are strongly temperature-dependent; at a constant incubation temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], embryos complete development and hatch after about 37.6 days [ab = about 37.6 days]. In contrast, when eggs are maintained at a warmer 24.5 °C [T = 24.5 °C], the incubation period shortens dramatically to roughly 12.7 days [ab = roughly 12.7 days], a nearly threefold acceleration that underscores the profound influence of thermal conditions on early developmental rates in this endemic Sardinian stream-dwelling salamander. The wet body mass of a freshly emerged larva is only 0.0141 grams [Wwb = 0.0141 grams], a value consistent with the species' modest egg diameter of approximately 3 mm and the limited yolk reserves available to support the initial lecithotrophic larval phase before the onset of exogenous feeding.

Following hatching, the free-swimming tadpoles enter a prolonged endotrophic phase characterized by yolk absorption before they begin active feeding. Metamorphosis, the dramatic morphological transformation that includes limb bud development, gill resorption, and skin keratinisation, occurs once individuals reach a snout–vent length of approximately 1.13 centimeters . Under captive conditions maintained at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the time elapsed since hatching to reach this developmental milestone is roughly 415 days , a notably protracted larval period compared to many other European salamandrids. However, when water temperatures are elevated to 20.5 °C [T = 20.5 °C], this larval duration is substantially compressed to about 210 days , indicating that thermal conditions can nearly halve the pre-metamorphic growing period. This plasticity in developmental rate likely reflects an adaptation to the cool, montane streams of Sardinia, where seasonal temperature fluctuations can be pronounced, and a faster rate under warmer conditions may confer a survival advantage by reducing the time spent in the aquatic, gill-breathing larval stage.

Upon completing metamorphosis, the terrestrial juveniles—or metamorphlings—enter a phase of rapid somatic growth that continues until they attain sexual maturity. Puberty, defined here as the onset of gonadal maturation and gametogenesis onset, is reached at a snout–vent length of approximately 3.6 centimeters [Lp = approximately 3.6 centimeters]. The time required from hatching to achieve this body size under a constant temperature regime of 15 °C [T = 15 °C] is approximately 1,460 days, or four years (1460 days after hatching) [tp = 1460 days after hatching]. Concurrently, the wet body mass at this pubertal stage is about 0.71 grams [Wwp = about 0.71 grams], a value that scales predictably from the adult body size relationships observed in this species. This relatively late maturation is characteristic of a slow life-history pace, typical of many island-endemic urodeles that experience low predation pressure and stable resource availability in their headwater stream habitats.

Adults of Euproctus platycephalus exhibit pronounced sexual size dimorphism, with males attaining a larger ultimate body size than females. The maximum recorded snout–vent length for males is 5.35 centimeters [Li = 5.35 centimeters], whereas females reach a somewhat smaller asymptotic length of 4.74 centimeters [Li = 4.74 centimeters]. This dimorphism is also reflected in their respective ultimate wet body masses: females achieve a maximum adult weight of approximately 2.9 grams [Wwi = approximately 2.9 grams], while males can reach up to 5.1 grams [Wwi = up to 5.1 grams], nearly double that of the females. These size disparities likely relate to differences in reproductive behavior and energetics; males engage in prolonged amplexus and territorial defense, which may favor larger body size, whereas females allocate substantial resources to egg production, limiting their somatic growth. The oldest documented individuals in the wild, maintained under the thermal conditions of their native streams at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], have been recorded living for up to 4,380 days, or approximately 12 years [am = approximately 12 years], a considerable lifespan for a small-bodied amphibian and indicative of a slow, iteroparous life-history strategy adapted to the relatively stable but cool aquatic environments of Sardinian mountain streams.

Reproductive output in the Sardinian brook salamander is modest but consistent with a K-selected life-history strategy. Females produce a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], with clutch sizes ranging from 57 to 221 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 57 to 221 eggs per clutch], yielding a maximum annual reproductive rate when expressed under the cool conditions of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This low fecundity is offset by the relatively large egg size and the extended period of parental care, which includes guarding the gelatinous egg mass until hatching. The eggs are deposited in shallow, well-oxygenated riffles of perennial streams, where they are attached to the underside of submerged stones. The combination of a single annual reproductive event, a moderately large clutch size by salamandrid standards, and a long lifespan suggests that population turnover is slow and that the species is vulnerable to perturbations that affect adult survival or recruitment, such as introduced predators or habitat degradation from water abstraction.
